chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from some of our companions from Ibn Jumhur from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim from Abdullah ibn Abi Ya'fur said:

We were in Medina, and Zurara disputed with me regarding plucking and shaving the armpits. I said, 'Shaving is superior,' and Zurara said, 'Plucking is superior.' We requested permission to enter upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and he granted us entry while he was in the bathhouse applying [ointment], having already applied to both his armpits. I said to Zurara, 'That is enough for you,' but he said, 'Perhaps he did this for something that is not permissible for me to do.' He asked, 'What are you two?' I said, 'Zurara disputed with me regarding plucking and shaving the armpits, and I said shaving is superior.' He said, 'You have followed the Sunnah and Zurara erred; shaving is superior to plucking, and applying [ointment] is superior to shaving.' Then he said to us, 'Apply [it].' We said, 'We applied it three days ago.' He said, 'Reapply, for applying [ointment] is a purifier.'

And we have clarified that the bath at the time of entering the state of Ihram is superior, and there is no harm in performing the bath before reaching the Miqat, so that one remains in that state until reaching the Miqat, then enters Ihram, provided one has not slept or passed a day and night. He narrated that.
ai.seo_question: What is the preferred method for removing armpit hair according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from the *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the practical jurisprudence of the Imams, specifically Imam al-Sadiq’s preference for shaving over plucking and the superior efficacy of applying ointment (itla’) as a form of ritual purification (tahur). It contextualizes these grooming practices within the broader framework of Hajj, noting that performing the bath before reaching the Miqat is preferable to maintain ritual state until the formal entry into Ihram.
